statement.p:
You break your piggy-bank to discover lots of pennies and nickels. You start arranging these in rows of 12 coins.
You find yourself making rows containing an equal number of pennies and nickels. For fun, you decide to lay out every possible such row. How many coins will you need?
How many coins would you need to make all possible rows of 12 coins (not necessarily with equal number of pennies and nickels)?

li.p: We can think of each row as a 12-bit string of weight 6 (since of the 12 coins, we require 6 to be pennies). Thus there are {12 \choose 6} = {924} rows possible. Each row requires 12 coins, so if we want to make all the rows at the same time, we will need 11088 coins, half of them nickels and half of them pennies.

Now there are 2^{12} = 4096 rows possible, which is also {12 \choose 0} + {12\choose 1} + {12 \choose 2} +\dots + {12 \choose 12}\text{,} if you break them up into rows containing 0, 1, 2, etc. pennies. Thus, since there are 12 coins in each row, we need 12 \cdot 4096 = {49152} total coins.
